lessons.title: How to Write Your First Resume
lessons.description: Learn how to build a resume from scratch — even with zero work experience. We'll cover formatting, what to include, and how to stand out.

video.title: How To Write A Resume With No Experience (Step By Step)

key_points: Your resume should fit on ONE page
List volunteer work, clubs, and school projects if you have no job experience
Use action verbs like: managed, created, organized, assisted
Always tailor your resume to the job description
Proofread at least 3 times before submitting

questions.question: How many pages should a first resume be?
questions.explanation: For young workers with limited experience, keep your resume to ONE page. Employers spend only 6–7 seconds scanning it.

questions.question: Which of these is the BEST action verb to start a resume bullet point?
questions.explanation: 'Managed' is a strong action verb. Avoid weak phrases like 'was responsible for' or vague words like 'did'.

questions.question: You have no work experience. What SHOULD you include on your resume?
options: Make up a job you didn't have
Include school projects, volunteer work, and clubs
Skip the resume and just show up in person
questions.explanation: School projects, extracurriculars, volunteer work, and babysitting all count as experience for a first resume!

questions.question: What does 'tailoring your resume' mean?
options: Adjusting your resume to match each specific job posting
Adding a photo to your resume
questions.explanation: Tailoring means reading the job description and using similar keywords and highlighting relevant skills for THAT specific job.

questions.question: Which section should appear at the TOP of a first resume?
questions.explanation: Always start with your name and contact info (email, phone, borough/city). Employers need to know who you are and how to reach you.

interactive_game.title: Build a Resume Section
interactive_game.instructions: Drag the correct items into the right resume sections.

lessons.title: Writing a Cover Letter That Gets Noticed
lessons.description: A strong cover letter can be the difference between getting an interview or not. Learn the 3-paragraph structure that actually works.

video.title: How To Write The BEST Cover Letter For a Job Application

key_points: Opening: Hook the reader — why YOU for THIS job?
Middle: Highlight 2–3 specific skills with examples
Closing: Express enthusiasm and ask for the interview
Keep it under 300 words
Never start with 'My name is...' — it's boring

questions.question: How long should a cover letter ideally be?
options: The same length as your resume
questions.explanation: A cover letter should be concise — under 300 words. Hiring managers are busy and won't read a long letter.

questions.question: What's the WORST way to start a cover letter?
options: 'My name is John and I am applying...'
questions.explanation: Starting with 'My name is...' is one of the most generic openers. The employer already knows your name from your resume!

questions.question: Should you send the same cover letter to every employer?
options: No, customize it for each job
questions.explanation: Always customize your cover letter! Mention the company name, the specific role, and why you're interested in THEIR organization.

questions.question: What should your closing paragraph do?
options: Ask for the interview and thank them
questions.explanation: Always close by expressing enthusiasm and explicitly asking for the interview. Don't be shy — 'I'd love the opportunity to discuss this role' works great.

interactive_game.title: Complete the Cover Letter
interactive_game.instructions: Choose the best word to fill in each blank of this cover letter paragraph.

paragraphs.text: I am _____ to apply for the Summer Internship at NYC Youth Works. As a Brooklyn native with a passion for community _____, I believe I would be a great fit for your team.
During my time as a volunteer at my school's food drive, I _____ a team of 8 students and helped _____ over 500 meals to families in need.

lessons.title: Nailing Your Job Interview
lessons.description: From what to wear to what to say — get fully prepared for your first job interview. Practice answering the most common questions hiring managers ask.
key_points: Arrive 10–15 minutes early — never late
Research the company before you go
Use the STAR method for behavioral questions
Ask 2–3 thoughtful questions at the end
Send a thank-you email within 24 hours

questions.question: What does STAR stand for in interview answers?
questions.explanation: STAR = Situation, Task, Action, Result. Use this framework to structure answers to behavioral questions like 'Tell me about a time when...'

questions.question: How early should you arrive to a job interview?
questions.explanation: 10–15 minutes early shows you're punctual and respectful. Arriving too early (30+ min) can actually be awkward for the interviewer.

questions.question: The interviewer asks 'What's your greatest weakness?' — what's the BEST response?
options: A real weakness you're actively working to improve
questions.explanation: Be honest but strategic. Pick a real weakness AND explain what you're doing to improve it. This shows self-awareness and growth mindset.

questions.question: What should you do within 24 hours of an interview?
options: Call them every hour for an update
Nothing — wait for them to contact you
Connect with the interviewer on social media
questions.explanation: A short, professional thank-you email shows gratitude and keeps you top of mind. Most candidates skip this — it's an easy way to stand out!

questions.question: At the end of an interview, the hiring manager says 'Do you have any questions?' You should:
options: Say 'No, I'm good' to seem easygoing
Ask 2–3 thoughtful questions about the role or company
Ask about salary and vacation days immediately
Ask if you got the job
questions.explanation: Always have questions ready! It shows genuine interest. Good ones: 'What does success look like in this role?' or 'What's the team culture like?'

questions.question: What should you research before an interview?
options: The company's mission, products/services, and recent news
How much the company is worth
questions.explanation: Research the company's website, what they do, their values, and any recent news. This helps you answer 'Why do you want to work here?' confidently.

interactive_game.title: Mock Interview Simulator
interactive_game.instructions: Read each interview question and pick the BEST response. You're interviewing for a retail job at a NYC clothing store.
interactive_game.scenario: You're interviewing for a part-time sales associate position at a NYC clothing boutique.

options.text: I'm 17, I love fashion, and I've always wanted to work in retail. I'm a junior at Brooklyn Tech and captain of the debate team, which taught me how to communicate confidently with people.
options.feedback: Perfect! You kept it professional, relevant, and showed transferable skills.

options.text: I don't know, I'm just a regular person. I go to school.
options.feedback: Too vague! Use this chance to make a great first impression.

options.text: I need money for college so that's why I'm here.
options.feedback: Honest but not professional. Focus on what you bring to THEM, not what you need.

options.text: I'm the best candidate you'll interview today, guaranteed.
options.feedback: Overconfident without evidence. Be enthusiastic, not arrogant.

rounds.question: Why do you want to work here specifically?

options.text: I shopped here before and love the style. I researched your brand and know you focus on sustainable fashion, which aligns with my values. I want to be part of a team that sells clothes I actually believe in.
options.feedback: Excellent! You showed you did research and connected your values to theirs.

options.text: It's close to my house.
options.feedback: Too casual. Location can be a factor, but lead with enthusiasm for the brand.

options.text: I applied everywhere. You just happened to call back.
options.feedback: Never say this! It signals you're not genuinely interested in their company.

options.text: The pay seems decent.
options.feedback: Salary is important, but don't lead with it in early interviews. Show passion first.

rounds.question: Describe a time you had to deal with a difficult person.

options.text: In my debate class, a teammate and I disagreed on strategy. I listened to their perspective, we found a compromise, and we ended up winning the round. I learned that conflict often leads to better outcomes.
options.feedback: Great STAR answer! Situation, action, and positive result.

options.text: My little brother is really annoying.
options.feedback: Keep it professional! Use a school or community example, not a personal family story.

options.text: I've never had a conflict with anyone.
options.feedback: This isn't believable and misses an opportunity to show your problem-solving skills.

options.text: I just ignore difficult people.
options.feedback: Avoidance isn't a good strategy in a customer-facing role. Show how you engage and resolve.

lessons.title: Workplace Communication 101
lessons.description: Texting your friends is totally different from communicating at work. Learn how to write professional emails, speak up in meetings, and handle workplace conversations.

video.title: Communication Skills - How To Improve Communication Skills

key_points: Use clear subject lines in emails: 'Question about Thursday schedule'
Start emails with a greeting: 'Hi [Name],' — not 'Hey' or nothing
Be direct and get to the point quickly
Read the room — know when to speak up vs. listen
Always respond to work messages within 24 hours

questions.question: Your manager texts you about a schedule change. What's the best reply?
options: 'Thanks for letting me know! I'll be there at 3pm.'
Don't reply — they'll figure it out
questions.explanation: Always acknowledge work messages professionally. Confirm the key detail (time, task) so your manager knows you understood.

questions.question: You disagree with your supervisor's idea. What do you do?
options: Say nothing and complain to coworkers
Yell at them to make your point
Respectfully say 'Could I share a different perspective?' and explain your thinking
questions.explanation: It's okay to disagree — the KEY is doing it respectfully and at the right time. Ask for permission to share, then make your case calmly.

questions.question: Which email subject line is most professional?
questions.explanation: Good subject lines are specific and clear. Including your name helps managers who receive many emails find yours quickly.

questions.question: You make a mistake at work. What's the professional response?
options: Acknowledge the mistake, apologize, and explain how you'll fix it
questions.explanation: Everyone makes mistakes. What matters is owning it, apologizing, and having a solution ready. This builds trust with your employer.

questions.question: A customer is being rude to you at work. You should:
options: Be rude back — they started it
Stay calm, listen, and try to solve their issue. If escalated, get a supervisor.
questions.explanation: Staying calm under pressure is one of the most valued workplace skills. Never match a customer's negative energy — de-escalate and involve a supervisor if needed.

interactive_game.title: Fix the Unprofessional Email
interactive_game.instructions: This email is terrible. Find all 5 mistakes and fix them to make it professional.

original_email.subject: hey
original_email.body: hey so i cant come in tomorrow because i dont feel good. also can i get friday off too? let me know asap. bye

mistakes.description: No explanation or advance notice for time off request

corrected_email.subject: Sick Day Request — [Your Name], Tuesday 5/20
corrected_email.body:
Hi [Manager's Name],

I wanted to let you know that I'm not feeling well and won't be able to come in tomorrow, Tuesday May 20th. I'm sorry for the short notice.

I also wanted to ask — would it be possible to have Friday, May 22nd off? I'd be happy to switch shifts with someone if needed.

Thank you so much for understanding.

Best,
[Your Name]

lessons.title: Understanding Your First Paycheck
lessons.description: Why does your paycheck look smaller than you expected? Learn about taxes, deductions, FICA, and how to actually read your pay stub.

video.title: How To Read A Pay Stub

key_points: Gross pay = what you earned before deductions
Net pay = what you actually take home (after taxes)
Federal & NY State income tax, Social Security, and Medicare are deducted
Your W-4 form controls how much federal tax is withheld
Keep all your pay stubs — you'll need them for taxes

questions.question: You earn $15/hr and work 20 hours this week. Your gross pay is $300. Your paycheck is $248. What happened?
options: Taxes and deductions were taken out
You were fined for being late
questions.explanation: The difference between gross pay ($300) and net pay ($248) is taxes and deductions — federal income tax, state tax, Social Security, and Medicare.

questions.question: What is FICA?
options: Federal Insurance Contributions Act — Social Security and Medicare taxes
A form you fill out when you quit
questions.explanation: FICA is a mandatory payroll tax that funds Social Security and Medicare. Everyone pays it — even teenagers on their first job.

questions.question: What is a W-2 form?
options: A form you fill out when you start a job
An annual summary of your earnings and taxes, sent by your employer
questions.explanation: Your employer sends you a W-2 every January. It shows your total earnings and taxes paid in the previous year. You need it to file your taxes.

questions.question: What form do you fill out when you START a new job to control tax withholding?
questions.explanation: The W-4 (Employee's Withholding Certificate) is filled out when you start a job. It tells your employer how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck.

questions.question: NYC minimum wage in 2025 is $16.50/hr. You work 15 hours a week for 8 weeks. What is your total GROSS earnings?
questions.explanation: $16.50 × 15 hrs × 8 weeks = $1,980 gross. (Your net take-home will be lower after taxes.)

interactive_game.instructions: Read the pay stub below and answer the questions about it.

questions.question: What is Jordan's net (take-home) pay this period?

lessons.title: Budgeting on Your First Income
lessons.description: You got your first paycheck — now what? Learn the 50/30/20 budgeting rule and how to save money even on a part-time income.

video.title: Budgeting for Beginners — How to Budget Money on a Low Income

key_points: 50% Needs: MetroCard, food, phone bill
30% Wants: eating out, clothes, entertainment
20% Savings: emergency fund, future goals
Track every dollar — even small purchases add up
Automate your savings so you don't skip it

questions.question: Using the 50/30/20 rule with a $500/month income, how much should go to savings?
questions.explanation: 20% of $500 = $100 for savings. Even $100/month adds up to $1,200 in a year!

questions.question: Which of these is a NEED, not a want?
questions.explanation: A MetroCard to get to work is a NEED. Streaming, dining out, and fashion are wants (even if they feel essential!).

questions.question: What's the smartest first savings goal for a teen?
options: Save up for a designer bag
questions.explanation: An emergency fund ($500–$1,000) is the foundation of financial security. It protects you when unexpected costs hit — like phone repairs or medical bills.

questions.question: You spend $8 on coffee 4 times a week. How much is that per year?
questions.explanation: $8 × 4 days × 52 weeks = $1,664/year! Small daily expenses add up dramatically. Brewing at home could save you over $1,000.

interactive_game.title: Build Your Monthly Budget
interactive_game.instructions: You earn $600/month after taxes. Allocate your money using the 50/30/20 rule. Drag the slider for each category.

lessons.title: Professional Email & Digital Communication
lessons.description: Learn how to write professional emails, use Slack/Teams effectively, and manage your digital workplace presence.

video.title: How to Write a Professional Email

key_points: Use a professional email address (firstname.lastname@gmail.com)
Always include a subject line that summarizes your email
Keep emails under 150 words when possible
Reply within 24 hours — even if just to say 'Got it, I'll respond soon'
Proofread before sending — autocorrect makes embarrassing mistakes

questions.question: Which is the most professional email address to use for job applications?
questions.explanation: firstname.lastname@gmail.com is clean, professional, and easy to remember. Avoid nicknames, birth years, or extra numbers.

questions.question: You receive an email from a hiring manager. When should you reply?
options: Only if you want the job
After a week — you don't want to seem desperate
questions.explanation: Reply within 24 hours to show professionalism. Even a quick 'Thank you for reaching out — I'll send my full response by tomorrow' is better than silence.

questions.question: Your coworker sends you a message on Slack with a question. Emojis are:
options: Never appropriate in any workplace communication
Context-dependent — okay in casual team chats, avoid in formal communications
Better than words in all situations
questions.explanation: Read the room! Emojis in casual Slack channels or team chats are often fine. In formal emails or messages to executives, keep it text-only.

questions.question: True or False: Employers often Google candidates before interviews. Your social media can affect your chances.
options: True — 70%+ of employers screen social media
False — employers are not allowed to look you up
Only if you're applying for a tech job
questions.explanation: TRUE! Over 70% of employers search candidates online. Google yourself now. Clean up public posts that could seem unprofessional.

lessons.title: Workplace Rights for Young Workers in NYC
lessons.description: Know your rights! NYC has strong protections for young workers. Learn about minimum wage, break requirements, working papers, and what to do if your rights are violated.

video.title: Know Your Rights as a Young Worker

key_points: NYC minimum wage is $16.50/hr (2025) for most workers
Workers under 18 need working papers (Employment Certificate) for most jobs
You're entitled to a 30-minute unpaid break for shifts over 6 hours
Employers CANNOT pay you less than minimum wage — even in cash
If your rights are violated, contact NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection

questions.question: Your employer says they can pay you $12/hr because 'you're still learning.' This is:
options: Okay — employers can set any training wage
Illegal — NYC minimum wage applies to all workers
Fine if you signed a contract
questions.explanation: NYC minimum wage ($16.50/hr in 2025) applies to all workers. You cannot legally be paid less, even during training. If this happens, contact the NYC Dept. of Consumer & Worker Protection.

questions.question: You're 16 and want to work. What document do you likely need?
questions.explanation: In NY, most workers under 18 need an Employment Certificate (working papers) from their school. Your school's main office can help you get them.

questions.question: You work a 7-hour shift. Are you legally entitled to a break?
questions.explanation: In New York, workers are entitled to a 30-minute unpaid meal break for shifts over 6 hours. For shifts over 11 hours, an additional 20-minute break is required.

questions.question: Your boss threatens to fire you for reporting a safety issue. This is called:
questions.explanation: Retaliation for reporting workplace issues (safety, harassment, wage theft) is illegal in NYC. You can report it to the NYC Commission on Human Rights or the NLRB.

questions.question: Your employer pays you 'under the table' in cash. Do you still need to pay taxes?
options: Yes — all income must be reported to the IRS, regardless of payment method
Only if you earn more than $10,000/year
Only if your employer sends a W-2
questions.explanation: ALL income is taxable — cash, checks, or apps. If your employer pays cash and doesn't withhold taxes, you may owe them yourself at tax time. Report all income.

interactive_game.title: What Would You Do?
interactive_game.instructions: Read each workplace scenario and choose the best course of action.

scenarios.situation: Your manager asks you to stay 3 hours past your scheduled time without pay. They say 'it's just this once.'

options.text: Stay and work for free to avoid conflict
options.feedback: Wage theft is illegal even 'just this once.' If unpaid overtime becomes a pattern, you have the right to report it.

options.text: Politely say you're happy to stay but need to confirm overtime pay, then document it in writing
options.feedback: Perfect! Document everything in writing. Overtime (over 40 hrs/week) must be paid at 1.5x your rate in NY.

options.text: Quit on the spot
options.feedback: Too extreme for a first offense. Try to address it directly first, and document if it continues.

options.text: Agree but call out sick the next day as revenge
options.feedback: This could get you fired for a legitimate reason. Address the real issue professionally.

scenarios.situation: A coworker keeps making jokes that make you uncomfortable and feel like harassment.

options.text: Laugh it off so you don't cause drama
options.feedback: You don't have to tolerate harassment. Laughing it off may signal it's okay to continue.

options.text: Calmly tell them their comments make you uncomfortable, document the incidents, and report to HR if it continues
options.feedback: This is exactly right. Set a boundary directly, document, and escalate if needed.

options.text: Post about it on social media
options.feedback: This can hurt your case legally and may violate workplace policies.

options.text: Quit without saying anything
options.feedback: You have rights! Don't let harassment drive you from a job. Report it through proper channels first.

scenarios.situation: You notice your paycheck is $50 short from what you calculated.

options.text: Assume you made a math mistake and say nothing
options.feedback: Always verify pay discrepancies! Keep records of your hours worked every day.

options.text: Calmly bring your records to your manager and ask them to review the calculation
options.feedback: Correct! Keep a log of your hours and compare it to your pay stub. Politely raise discrepancies — most are honest mistakes.

options.text: Take $50 worth of merchandise to make up for it
options.feedback: This is theft and could get you arrested. Always resolve pay issues through proper channels.

options.text: Post a bad review of the company immediately
options.feedback: Try to resolve internally first. If they refuse to fix it, then you can escalate to the NYC Dept. of Consumer & Worker Protection.

lessons.title: Time Management & Showing Up Strong
lessons.description: Balancing school, work, social life, and sleep is hard. Learn practical time management strategies that actually work for young workers.

video.title: Time Management for Students & Young Professionals

key_points: Use a weekly calendar to block out work, school, and study time
Prioritize tasks by urgency AND importance (Eisenhower Matrix)
The 2-minute rule: if it takes under 2 min, do it now
Batch similar tasks together to reduce mental switching
Protect your sleep — exhaustion kills productivity and professionalism

questions.question: You have a big test tomorrow AND a work shift tonight. What's the best strategy?
options: Study during your break at work and for 1 hour before your shift
Skip studying — you'll wing the test
Work all night then cram in the morning
questions.explanation: Plan ahead! Use small pockets of time efficiently. 1 hour of focused study before your shift + break time review beats frantic last-minute cramming.

questions.question: What does 'reliability' mean in the workplace?
options: Consistently showing up on time and doing what you say you'll do
questions.explanation: Reliability is showing up consistently, on time, and following through on commitments. It's one of the most valued traits in ANY entry-level employee.

questions.question: You're scheduled to work but a friend invited you to a party that night. You should:
options: Honor your work commitment; plan the party for another night
Just not show up without calling
Leave work early without telling anyone
questions.explanation: When you're scheduled to work, that's a commitment. Calling out for social events — especially without notice — damages your reputation and puts extra burden on coworkers.

lessons.title: LinkedIn & Online Presence for Young Professionals
lessons.description: LinkedIn isn't just for adults in suits — it's how young people get discovered by employers. Build a standout profile and start networking today.

video.title: LinkedIn Profile Tips for Students & New Graduates

key_points: Use a professional headshot — no sunglasses, group photos, or blurry selfies
Your headline should say MORE than just 'Student' — add your goal
Connect with teachers, counselors, coaches, and family in your field
The 'About' section is your personal pitch — make it compelling
Engage with posts — likes and comments increase your visibility

questions.question: Which LinkedIn headline is most effective for a student looking for a tech internship?
options: Brooklyn Tech Senior | Aspiring Software Developer | Python & Web Design
Looking for work!!! Please hire me
questions.explanation: Your headline should include your school, your goal, and 1–2 relevant skills. It's the first thing employers see when they find your profile.

questions.question: You have 0 connections on LinkedIn. Who should you connect with FIRST?
options: Random recruiters and CEOs you don't know
Teachers, school counselors, coaches, and family members
No one — just wait for employers to find you
questions.explanation: Start with your real-life network. Teachers, coaches, and family often have professional connections that can lead to opportunities.

questions.question: An employer Googles your name and finds your public Instagram with party photos. This:
options: Can hurt your chances if the content seems unprofessional
Only matters if you're applying for a government job
Actually helps — shows you're fun and social
questions.explanation: Over 70% of employers check social media. You don't have to delete everything — but make sure your public profile wouldn't make an employer question your judgment.

questions.question: When reaching out to someone new on LinkedIn to ask about opportunities, you should:
options: Just say 'Hi, can you get me a job?'
Send a personalized note mentioning a specific reason you're reaching out and something you genuinely admire about their work
questions.explanation: Personalized messages dramatically increase response rates. Reference something specific: their career path, a post they wrote, or your shared school.

lessons.title: Networking 101: Building Real Connections
lessons.description: 70% of jobs are never posted online — they're filled through connections. Learn how to network authentically without feeling fake or pushy.

video.title: How to Network (Even If You Hate Networking)

key_points: Networking = building genuine relationships, not just collecting contacts
Your elevator pitch should be 30–60 seconds: who you are, what you do, what you're looking for
Ask for advice, not jobs — people love helping
Follow up within 48 hours of meeting someone
Give before you ask — share articles, make introductions, add value

questions.question: What percentage of jobs are estimated to be filled through networking?
questions.explanation: Studies suggest 70-80% of jobs are filled through networking and referrals — many are never even posted publicly. Your network is your most powerful career tool.

questions.question: You're at a career fair and want to ask someone for help. Which is the BEST approach?
options: 'Do you have any jobs for me?'
'I'm interested in your field — could I ask for 10 minutes of advice on how you got started?'
'Can you look at my resume right now?'
questions.explanation: Asking for advice is far more effective than asking for a job. People love sharing their stories and are more likely to remember — and help — someone who shows genuine curiosity.

questions.question: What's an 'elevator pitch'?
options: A pitch for a startup on an elevator
A 30–60 second professional introduction of who you are and what you're looking for
A list of all your accomplishments
An email template for job applications
questions.explanation: An elevator pitch is a brief, polished introduction you can deliver in the time it takes to ride an elevator — about 30–60 seconds. Practice yours until it feels natural.

lessons.title: Filing Taxes for the First Time
lessons.description: Taxes don't have to be scary! Learn how to file your first tax return, what forms you need, and free resources for NYC youth.

video.title: How to File Taxes for the First Time — Step by Step

key_points: Tax deadline is usually April 15th each year
You need your W-2 form from your employer to file
Most teens can file for FREE using IRS Free File or NYC Free Tax Prep
If you're a dependent, your parents may claim you — still file your own return
You may get a refund — don't leave money on the table!

questions.question: When is the federal tax filing deadline (in most years)?
questions.explanation: April 15th is Tax Day! If you miss it without filing an extension, you may face penalties. Mark your calendar.

questions.question: What is a tax refund?
options: Money you borrow from the government
A penalty for not paying taxes
Money returned to you if you overpaid taxes throughout the year
questions.explanation: If more taxes were withheld from your paychecks than you actually owed, the government sends you the difference back as a refund. File on time so you don't miss it!

questions.question: NYC offers free tax preparation for individuals earning under a certain amount. This service is called:
questions.explanation: NYC Free Tax Prep (part of the IRS VITA program) offers free, professional tax filing for qualifying New Yorkers. Visit nyc.gov/taxprep to find a site near you.

questions.question: You're 17 and your parents claim you as a dependent. Do you still need to file taxes?
options: No — your parents file for you automatically
Yes — if you earned over $13,850 (2024), you must file your own return too
Only if you had a full-time job
questions.explanation: Even dependents must file their own tax return if they earn above the standard deduction threshold ($13,850 in 2024). You may also want to file even with less income to get any withheld taxes refunded.

interactive_game.title: Match the Tax Form
interactive_game.instructions: Draw a line matching each tax form to its correct description.
